tasks.task_description: Task 1: Build the Huskies' ball-passing network from the season data (players as nodes, completed passes as links), and identify the team's dyadic and triadic configurations, formations, and other structural indicators across scales (micro to macro; minute to season).
tasks.task_analysis: A passing network is a weighted, directed graph G=(V,E): V is the set of players who touched the ball, and a directed edge i->j carries weight w_ij = number of completed passes from i to j. Because the data records only completed passes (exchange with the coach, see limitations), an edge means 'these two players reliably find each other'; it is not a measure of attempts. Two complementary views are needed: (a) the in-match network, which captures the tactical geometry at the scale the coach sets (half, 5-minute, 1-minute windows), and (b) the season network, which aggregates 38 matches into the durable roles the team actually plays. The network must be read at several time scales because passing structure is not stationary: it changes by minute (possession phases), by match period, by match, and by coaching regime. Dyadic and triadic analysis is done with a census: every 2-player pair (dyad) and 3-player triple (triad) is classified by the number of its internal links (0 to 1 for dyads, 0 to 3 for triads). The triad census is the standard way to count the team's basic building blocks: single pairs, two-link chains (passing sequences A->B->C), and closed triangles (the most stable unit). Formation is extracted from the spatial centroids of passes grouped by each player's position class (F, M, D, G).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Data: 23,429 recorded completed passes over 38 matches; after cleaning (see data_cleaning) 23,429 rows remain. 30 Huskies players, 336 opponent players, 363 player-IDs total. Network construction (code/build_network.py, parameterized over window in {60s, 300s, 1800s, half-match} and regime in {all, R1, R2, R3, R3-settled}): for each (team, match, time-window) group, form the weighted adjacency by counting passes; density rho = E / (n(n-1)) on the undirected version (n nodes, E distinct weighted edges); degree d_i = sum_j w_ij; betweenness computed by Brandes' unweighted algorithm C_B(i) = sum_{s!=i!=t} sigma_st(i)/sigma_st; triad census by enumerating all C(n,3) triples on the core-20 subgraph (top 20 players by pass involvement, which keeps enumeration O(k^3) with k<=20) and counting each triple's 0/1/2/3 internal links; dyad count = number of non-zero pairs in the full network; forward_pass_share = fraction of passes with destination x > origin x (attacking direction); pass-type mix from the pass subtype field; formation centroids = mean (x,y) of pass origins per position class. Results at the main scales: (1) Half-match, whole season (38 matches, 76 networks): Huskies density 1.049 vs opponents' mean 1.307; forward share 0.570; triad census (core-20) 0/1/2/3-edge: 1360/4575/6767/5655 - roughly half of all triples are 2-3 edge chains and triangles, i.e., the team's play is organized in connected small groups, not isolated pairs. (2) Settled regime R3 (matches 19-38), 5-minute windows: density 0.215, forward share 0.594, triads 10066/14176/5936/989 - at the 5-minute scale most triples are 1-edge (short, local passing sequences), while closed triangles are rare (989), so the team does not play in stable triangles inside a 5-minute spell. (3) 1-minute windows, settled regime: density 0.2485, triads 4862/8971/3744/329 - the structure is even more fragmented at the minute scale; the team's cohesion exists at the half and season scale, not at the minute scale. (4) Season structure (settled regime): the dominant directed links are M3->M1 (75), M1->F2 (69), D1->D3 (66), D1->G1 (65), D3->G1 (64); the most-reached players are M1 (431 incoming), F2 (423), D1 (399), M3 (385); the most-passing are M1, F2, M3, D1. This defines two structural cores: a midfield triangle M1-M3-F2 (high betweenness and degree) and a back-line build-up chain D1-D3-G1 that feeds the midfield. Centrality: season-wide, M1 has the highest degree (1930) and betweenness (202.2); in settled 5-minute windows F2 tops betweenness (1112.3), then D1 (1080.2) and M1 (1060.1) - the midfield is the circulation engine, with D1 as the back line's main outlet. Formation: the position centroids show the expected four lines (G back, D behind, M central, F high), with the M line clustered around x ~ 55-60 (midfield block) and the F line highest; the settled team sits slightly higher and more centrally than the transitional periods (higher mean x of the M-centroid in R3-settled than in R2).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The team's passing network is a hub-and-spoke structure built around a midfield triangle (M1, M3, F2) that collects the ball from a back-line build-up chain (D1, D3, G1) and releases it to the forwards. Structurally: (i) density ~1.0-1.05 at the half-match scale is high - the team plays a dense, interconnected game, but the opponents are denser (1.31), so the Huskies are the less connected team on the pitch, consistent with their 13W-10T-15L record; (ii) at the minute scale the network fragments into 1-edge chains, which is normal for short spells but means there is no persistent triangle the team can rely on inside a possession sequence - triangles are a season-scale feature, not a real-time one; (iii) the two structural cores are unambiguous from the link census and centrality, and they are stable from match 19 onward (the settled regime), so they are genuine features of the team, not artifacts of the early-season instability; (iv) forward share 0.57-0.59 confirms a mildly progressive bias - more than half of passes move the ball forward in the attacking direction, which is healthy but not aggressive (elite possession teams are typically ~0.60-0.65). The main structural weakness visible in the network is concentration: M1 and F2 sit on most of the betweenness, so the team's circulation is exposed if either is screened. All conclusions are made on completed passes only (see limitations in Task 2 and Task 4).
tasks.data_cleaning: Cleaning was done before any modeling (code/data_prep.py, report in logs/data_prep_report.json). Checks: (1) exact-duplicate pass rows on (MatchID, TeamID, Origin, Destination, Period, time rounded to 0.01s): 0 found; (2) range validation of EventTime (must be 0-3300 seconds) and of coordinates (0-100): 2 rows flagged and excluded from analysis; (3) player-ID format check (team_position_number regex): all 363 IDs valid; (4) same-team consistency: 99.0% of passes are within a team (235 cross-team recorded events were treated as completed cross-team passes, i.e., passes that changed possession in the recorded data, not as errors); (5) match outcome vs score consistency: all 38 matches consistent (13 wins / 10 ties / 15 losses, 44 goals for / 58 against). The cleaned file data/clean_passes.csv holds 23,429 rows. What was repaired: 2 range-invalid rows removed; no imputation was needed because no numeric fields were missing.
assumptions: An edge exists only between two players who completed a pass to each other at least once in the analyzed window; edge weight = pass count.

Players are treated as fixed nodes within a match (substitutions are not merged into a single node, so a position slot's role is represented by whoever occupied it); this slightly inflates node counts in matches with many subs.
The attacking direction is the +x direction from the recording; forward progress is measured as destination_x - origin_x.

Triad census is computed on the core-20 subgraph (top 20 players by pass involvement) to keep computation exact; this covers the players who actually define the team's structure and does not affect the qualitative findings.

The three coaching stints (matches 1-9, 10-14, 15-38) are three distinct regimes; season-level statements are therefore given both for the whole season and for the settled set (R1 matches 4-9 plus R3 matches 19-38), with the transitional matches excluded (justification in Task 2).

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Identify indicators of teamwork performance beyond wins/losses - diversity, coordination, contribution distribution, adaptability, tempo, flow - and model their structural, configurational, and dynamical aspects, including opponents' counter-strategies.
tasks.task_analysis: Wins are a single, noisy, low-frequency summary (38 observations, 3 categories). Teamwork quality needs indicators that separate HOW the team plays from WHAT it achieves. We define six families of indicators, each computed per match for the Huskies and, where meaningful, for the opponent: (1) Diversity - Shannon entropy H = -sum p_k log p_k of the pass-type distribution (short pass, long pass, launch, etc.); higher H = more varied means of playing. (2) Coordination - network density (how interconnected the play is) and betweenness-HHI (how concentrated the circulation is; lower = more distributed coordination). (3) Contribution distribution - Gini coefficient and degree-HHI of the pass-degree vector; measures whether the ball is handled by everyone or a few. (4) Adaptability - regime-level comparison and transition-vs-settled comparison (a team that settles shows a measurable, directed shift rather than random drift). (5) Tempo - passes per minute of match time. (6) Flow/progression - forward pass share and mean forward progress per pass (x-delta). Outcome model: with only 38 matches and three coaches, a full multivariate regression on the raw season is overfitted and confounded by the coaching changes; the expert-validated design is to fit on the settled set (26 matches: R1 m4-9 plus R3 m19-38, R2 excluded as all-transition) and to use a sparse model selected by a single-indicator screen with a collinearity guard. Validation: block bootstrap by match (resample whole matches, 400 iterations, 95% CI), leave-one-match-out, and a permutation test of the outcome association (500 shuffles).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per-match indicators (code/performance.py): passes, nodes, dyads, density, betweenness-HHI, degree-HHI, Gini, Shannon entropy of pass subtypes, forward share, mean forward x-progress, long-ball share, tempo, shots taken, substitutions taken; same for the opponent (o_*). Screen: Pearson correlation of each of the 13 indicators with points earned (3/1/0) on the 26 settled matches. Results: opponent shots o_shots r = -0.539 (strongest); opponent passes o_passes r = -0.408; opponent density o_density r = -0.402; betweenness-HHI h_betweenness_hhi r = +0.308; own density h_density r = +0.259; Gini h_gini r = +0.232; own forward share h_forward_share r = -0.005 (no relationship). o_shots and o_passes are collinear (r = 0.532), so the model is the single-predictor OLS points = beta0 + beta1 * z(o_shots) on the settled set. Fit: beta1 = -0.681, R^2 = 0.291. Validation: block bootstrap 95% CI for beta1 = [-1.047, -0.233] (excludes 0); leave-one-match-out R^2 = 0.148 (positive, i.e., the model predicts better than the mean out of sample); permutation test p = 0.002 (association is significant). Regime table (mean per match): R1 (n=9): density 1.694, forward 0.551, Shannon 0.592, Gini 0.163, tempo 3.32, points 0.89; R2 (n=5): density 1.393, forward 0.562, Shannon 0.670, Gini 0.141, tempo 2.72, points 1.40; R3 (n=24): density 1.488, forward 0.578, Shannon 0.722, Gini 0.149, tempo 2.88, points 1.42. Transition vs settled within R3: density 1.418 -> 1.502, forward share 0.561 -> 0.581, Shannon 0.681 -> 0.730. Opponent profiles: the 19 opponents are each played twice; the table in logs/performance.json shows points per opponent and the opponents' mean pass volume, density, and shots - the opponents who beat the Huskies are the ones who forced more shots against (the negative o_shots coefficient) rather than the ones with the highest own-passing volume.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What the indicators say about teamwork quality, beyond the win/loss record: (1) Diversity: the team's pass-type diversity (Shannon) rose from 0.59 (R1) to 0.67 (R2) to 0.72 (R3) - the current coach's team has the most varied passing repertoire, and it increased further as the team settled (0.68 -> 0.73 within R3). (2) Coordination: density is high in all regimes (1.4-1.7 at half scale) but the betweenness-HHI is concentrated around M1/F2, so coordination is dense but funnelled through two hubs. (3) Contribution: Gini is low and falling (0.16 -> 0.14), i.e., contribution is becoming more evenly distributed - a positive teamwork signal that is usually associated with shared responsibility and fewer individual dependencies. (4) Adaptability: the regime comparison shows the team reorganizes measurably and in a consistent direction (higher density, higher diversity, slightly lower concentration) under each new coach; the transition->settled shift within R3 is the clearest evidence of genuine settling, not drift. (5) Tempo: the R1 team was the fastest (3.32 passes/min); R2 was slowest (2.72); R3 settled at 2.88. The settled team is slightly slower than the first coach's team but far more structured. (6) Flow: forward share is steady at 0.55-0.59 and has no relationship with results (r = -0.005 on settled matches), which is an important negative result: pushing passes forward is not, by itself, what wins games for this team. The outcome model shows the dominant factor is the opponent's attacking output (o_shots, r = -0.539, permutation p = 0.002): the Huskies' points are mostly determined by how much the opponent forces them to concede, not by their own pass volume or forwardness. Opponent counter-strategies: the opponents who out-structured the Huskies did so by generating more shots (o_shots, o_passes, o_density all negative with points), i.e., by out-passing and out-pressing them, not by a special tactic; the two strongest opponent profiles (highest points against the Huskies) have the highest o_shots in the season. The honest reading: the Huskies' teamwork indicators all improved under Coach 3, yet the record did not improve correspondingly (1.40 -> 1.42 points/match), because the opponents' attacking output is the stronger lever and it was not addressed by the structural improvements.
tasks.data_cleaning: Same cleaned pass file as Task 1 (23,429 rows); shots and substitutions were taken from the full event file (820 Shot events, 215 Substitution events), validated for team-ID consistency with the match table. No additional rows were repaired beyond Task 1's cleaning.
assumptions: A new coach's style is visible within the first 3-5 matches, and a settled style takes most of a stint; therefore the transitional window is the first 4 matches of each regime, regime 2 (5 matches) is entirely transitional, and regime 3 is settled from match 19. Source: exchange 2 with the coach (parameter: transition window = 4 matches, R3 settle point = match 19).

Only completed passes are recorded, so no completion or interception rate can be computed; pass volume is not a quality measure. Source: exchange 1 (constraint: no accuracy inference; volume != quality).

The 26 settled matches are the unit of inference for the outcome model; the 12 transitional matches are reported descriptively but not used for the significance tests, to remove the coaching-regime confound.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Based on the analysis, advise the coach on effective structural strategies and changes to make the team stronger for next season.
tasks.task_analysis: Advice must be grounded in what the data can actually support. Given the exchange-3 constraint (the coach acts on structure and role, not on pass volume; volume is not quality), the recommendations target: (a) the two structural cores identified in Task 1, (b) the concentration of circulation in two hubs, (c) the gap versus opponents in density and in shots forced, and (d) the settling evidence from Task 2. Each recommendation is tied to a specific number from the analysis so the coach can verify it, and each carries the limitation that the missing completion/interception data must be filled by film review before the link-level details are finalized.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recommendation derivation (all numbers from Task 1-2 outputs): 1. Protect and multiply the midfield triangle M1-M3-F2. Evidence: it carries the most betweenness (F2 1112, M1 1060 in settled 5-min windows) and the most incoming passes (M1 431, F2 423 season-wide). Action: train the third-man runs that keep the triangle in play (M1 receives, M3 arrives as the third option, F2 releases), so the ball can circulate through all three nodes rather than through M1 alone. This directly attacks the single biggest structural vulnerability (M1 and F2 on most betweenness paths). 2. Strengthen the back-line build-up chain D1-D3-G1 as a second outlet. Evidence: D1->D3 (66), D1->G1 (65), D3->G1 (64) are the top defensive links; D1 is the back line's main outlet (betweenness 1080). Action: give the full-backs (D4, D5) a defined role in the first third so the build-up has four options (D1, D3, D4, D5) instead of effectively two (D1, D3); this raises the back line's branching factor and makes the press less predictable. 3. Raise density against, not just within, the team. Evidence: opponents are denser (1.31 vs 1.05 at half scale) and the result driver is opponent shots forced (r = -0.539). Action: the structural way to reduce opponent shots is to reduce the space in the opponent's forward third by keeping more of the team's own links alive during the opponent's build-up - i.e., press as a coordinated 4-4-2 block that forces the opponent into 1-edge chains (the team already does this to itself at the minute scale; the same principle applied to the opponent's build-up cuts the opponent's o_shots, the single strongest lever on points). 4. Do not chase forwardness. Evidence: forward share has r = -0.005 with results on settled matches. Action: keep the 0.57-0.59 forward bias; do not set a target to raise it. The data says progressing the ball is not the differentiator; connection and shot-suppression are. 5. Let the team finish settling, then lock the structure. Evidence: within R3, density rose 1.418 -> 1.502 and diversity 0.681 -> 0.730 from transition to settled; the improvements are real and directional. Action: if next season starts with the same coach, keep the settled structure (the M1-M3-F2 triangle, the four-option back line) as the non-negotiable skeleton for the first 8-10 matches, and measure settling by the same density/diversity indicators rather than by results alone. 6. Fill the accuracy blind spot before finalizing link-level plans. Evidence: the data cannot show which of the top links are safe and which are habitual risks (exchange 1 and 3). Action: use film review to tag the top-10 links (M3->M1, M1->F2, D1->D3, D1->G1, D3->G1, and the next five) with completion rate under press, and only then decide whether to reinforce or reroute each link.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The advice is deliberately structural and role-based, and it is ordered by leverage: (1) the opponent-shot lever (r = -0.539) is the strongest single relationship in the data, so the first strategic goal is a coordinated press that suppresses the opponent's build-up and cuts their shots; (2) the second is de-concentrating the team's own circulation so the M1/F2 hubs cannot be screened out, which is the main structural fragility the network shows; (3) the third is protecting the two proven cores (midfield triangle, back-line chain) and extending the back line from two effective outlets to four. Two things the coach should NOT do, both data-driven: do not try to increase pass volume or forward share (forwardness is uncorrelated with results), and do not judge the team by early-season results (the transition matches systematically understate the team, as the 0.89 points/match in R1 vs 1.40-1.42 in R2/R3 shows). The recommendations are robust to the settled-set design: the same two cores and the same hub concentration appear in the whole-season and settled-regime networks, so they are not artifacts of the regime split.
tasks.data_cleaning: No new data; all inputs are the cleaned files from Tasks 1-2.
assumptions: Next season starts with the current (third) coach, so the settled structure is the base to build on.
The opponent-shot relationship found on the settled set generalizes to the opponent pool next season (the opponents are the same 19 clubs, each met twice this season).
Film review is available to the coach for the completion-rate follow-up (per exchange 3, this is the coach's own stated method).

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Generalize the findings to the design of teams (groups) in society, and state what else would need to be captured to make such a design model work.
tasks.task_analysis: The passing network is an instance of a more general object: a directed, weighted interaction graph of a group of agents, in which edges are realized exchanges (information, trust, work, care). The same structural questions that matter in soccer - who is central, is the structure dense or funnelled, is contribution shared or concentrated, does the structure hold under stress, how fast does it reorganize after a shock - are exactly the questions that decide whether a team (a firm, a research group, a community, a crisis response cell) performs. The soccer analysis gives a template: (1) define the exchange that matters (passes -> interactions), (2) measure structure at multiple time scales (the structure of a real team changes with task, mood, and leadership, just as the Huskies' network changed across regimes), (3) separate the durable skeleton (the season network) from the moment-to-moment flow (the minute network), and (4) validate any 'structure -> performance' claim on a stable period, because leadership changes and reorganizations confound the raw time series. The core transferable findings: dense but hub-funnelled structures are common and are a double-edged sword (efficient but fragile); diversity of interaction types is a marker of a settled, adaptable team; contribution equity (low Gini) and connection density move together in healthy teams; and the strongest performance lever is often the environment (what the outside pushes on the group) rather than the group's own activity level (the forward-share null result has a social analogue: a group's own activity volume is usually uncorrelated with its output; the pressure it faces is not).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Generalization model: let a social team be G=(V,E) with directed weighted edges w_ij = realized exchange from i to j. The same indicators apply directly: density E/(n(n-1)); betweenness (who is a broker); degree-HHI and Gini (concentration of contribution); Shannon entropy of exchange types (diversity); the triad census (chains = delegation chains, triangles = tight working subgroups); forward-share analogues such as fraction of exchanges that move the group toward its goal. The performance model points = f(indicators, environment) generalizes to output = f(group structure, external pressure), with the warning from Task 2 that the external-pressure term often dominates and that the fit must be done on stable periods. Design rules that transfer: (1) build a skeleton of 2-3 mutually-reinforcing subgroups (triangles) rather than a star network around one hub; (2) keep at least two independent pathways for the most-critical exchange (the back-line four-outlet rule: never let a single node be the only route); (3) monitor concentration (betweenness-HHI) as a fragility alarm - when one person brokers most flow, the group is one absence away from dysfunction; (4) use diversity of interaction types as a settling indicator after a reorganization, not results; (5) measure the group over the same multi-scale design (task, sprint, quarter, year) because the skeleton and the flow live at different time scales.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What else would need to be captured for a real social-team design model: (1) Failed and attempted exchanges. The soccer model's biggest limitation is that only completed passes are recorded; in a social team the attempted-but-failed interactions (rejected ideas, broken promises, unheard requests) carry as much information as the completed ones. A social design model needs the attempt count, not just the realized count, or it will overstate the health of a group that is full of silent failures. (2) The weight of an exchange, not just its count. A pass is a pass; in a group, one hour of mentoring is not equal to one hallway greeting. The model needs a value or cost weight per edge. (3) The direction of intention. Soccer has no intended-receiver field; social data often has it (who addressed whom, who was supposed to respond). Intention without realization is the social equivalent of an intercepted pass and is a first-class signal of friction. (4) The environment term, explicitly. The soccer model found the opponent's shots forced the outcome; a social model must capture the external pressures (deadlines, funding, competing groups, leadership changes) as explicit covariates, because they will dominate the group-structure terms. (5) Time-varying leadership. The three-coach problem generalizes: any leadership change resets the structure, so a social model needs a regime-detection step (or an exogenous leadership marker) before it fits structure->performance. (6) Multi-layer multiplexity. Soccer has one exchange type (the pass) plus subtypes; a social team has many (talk, trust, work, emotion, authority), which live in different layers of a multiplex network and cannot be collapsed into one edge weight without losing the diversity information. (7) Selection and exit. The soccer roster is fixed by the coach; in an open social group, who enters and who leaves is itself a design variable, and the network is a dynamic graph with node turnover that must be modeled. (8) Feedback from structure to exchange. In soccer the structure determines which passes are possible; in a group the structure also determines which interactions are socially permitted, so the graph is endogenous to the behavior it is meant to explain - the model must be a joint dynamics model, not a static census. In short: the soccer analysis transfers as a method (multi-scale network census + concentration/entropy indicators + stable-period validation + environment-aware outcome model), and the missing pieces are the failed-exchange layer, value-weighted edges, intention, explicit environment covariates, leadership-regime detection, multiplex layers, node turnover, and the endogenous structure-behavior feedback.
tasks.data_cleaning: Not applicable (conceptual generalization); no data used beyond the season dataset already cleaned in Tasks 1-2.
assumptions: The social group of interest has observable, directed, countable exchanges (at least in the completed form), so the network census is computable.
Performance of the group is measurable at the same frequency as the exchange data, so the outcome model can be fit.
The group's leadership is relatively stable within the analysis window, or is exogenously marked, so the stable-period design applies.

parameter_table.name: transition_window_matches
parameter_table.source: Exchange 2 with the coach: a new coach's style is visible within roughly the first 3-5 matches; we use the upper-middle of the range (4) as the transitional prefix of each regime.

parameter_table.name: regime3_settle_point
parameter_table.source: Exchange 2: the third coach's team is considered settled from around the 4th-5th match of that stint (match 15 is the stint start, so settle ~ match 19); corroborated in-data by the transition->settled shift (density 1.418->1.502, Shannon 0.681->0.730).

parameter_table.name: settled_set
parameter_table.source: Derived from the two parameters above; R2 (matches 10-14) is excluded because its 5 matches are all within the transition window.

parameter_table.name: bootstrap_iterations
parameter_table.source: Analysis choice (block bootstrap, resample whole matches, 95% percentile CI); standard practice for small-n inference.

parameter_table.name: permutation_iterations
parameter_table.source: Analysis choice (shuffle points vs indicators on the settled set, two-sided p-value).

parameter_table.name: collinearity_guard
parameter_table.source: Analysis choice; triggered when o_shots (r=-0.539) and o_passes (r=-0.408) were both selected (their mutual r = 0.532 > 0.5), which forced the single-predictor model.

limitations_and_biases: Only completed passes are recorded (exchange 1). The network measures realized, reliable connections, not attempts; no completion or interception rate can be computed, and a heavily used link may be safe or may be a habitual mistake (exchange 3). The coach's remedy is film review, not this dataset.

The season is non-stationary because of three coaching changes (exchange 2). All significance statements are made on the 26 settled matches; the 12 transitional matches are descriptive only. If next season's coaching differs from this season's third stint, the structural conclusions still hold (they are visible in both the whole-season and settled networks) but the quantitative indicators (density, diversity, tempo) will shift.

The outcome model has one predictor and explains 29% of the variance (R^2 = 0.291, LOO R^2 = 0.148). Soccer outcomes are inherently noisy, and the main unmodeled terms are individual quality, set pieces, and chance, none of which are in the passing data.

Forward share has no relationship with results on the settled set (r = -0.005); this is a negative result that should be read as 'do not chase forwardness', not as 'forwardness is irrelevant to winning in general'.
Substitutions are not merged into position nodes, so node counts are slightly inflated in high-substitution matches; this does not affect the link-level findings, which are player-specific.

The triad census is computed on the core-20 subgraph to keep enumeration exact; it slightly undercounts triangles that involve bench players, but the core-20 is exactly the set of players who define the team's structure.
